changes.original: Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home. When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school.
changes.adaptation: Wangari’s big brother asked why she did not go to school with him. Her mother agreed to send her. Wangari later said she loved learning to read and write.

changes.original: When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry.
changes.adaptation: After her studies, Wangari returned to Kenya. She listened to rural women who needed firewood, food and clean water. Trees and streams that their families relied on were being lost.

changes.original: Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong.
changes.adaptation: Wangari worked with women to grow and plant trees. Their work became the Green Belt Movement. Together, they cared for the land and worked to improve life in their communities.

changes.original: As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds.
changes.adaptation: The movement grew. Women and their communities planted millions of trees in Kenya. People in other African countries took up the idea too.
